            - paragraph [ref=e417]:
              - text: The cat (
              - generic [ref=e418]: Felis catus
              - text: ), also called domestic cat and house cat, is a small domesticated
              - link "carnivorous" [ref=e419] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carnivore
              - text: mammal. It is a member of
              - link "Felidae" [ref=e420] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Felidae
              - text: ", the family of mammals in the"
              - link "order" [ref=e421] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Order_(taxonomy)
              - link "Carnivora" [ref=e422] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carnivora
              - text: also colloquially referred to as cats. An
              - link "obligate carnivore" [ref=e423] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Obligate_carnivore
              - text: ", requiring a predominantly meat-based diet, it has retractable"
              - link "claws" [ref=e424] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Claw
              - text: adapted to killing small prey species such as
              - link "mice" [ref=e425] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mice
              - text: and
              - link "rats" [ref=e426] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rat
              - text: . It has a strong, flexible body, quick
              - link "reflexes" [ref=e427] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reflex
              - text: ", and sharp teeth, and its"
              - link "night vision" [ref=e428] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Night_vision
              - text: and
              - link "sense of smell" [ref=e429] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sense_of_smell
              - text: are well developed. It is a
              - link "social species" [ref=e430] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Social_species
              - text: ", but a solitary hunter and a"
              - link "crepuscular" [ref=e431] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crepuscular
              - link "predator" [ref=e432] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Predator
              - text: .
              - link "Cat communication" [ref=e433] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cat_communication
              - text: includes
              - link "meowing" [ref=e434] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meow
              - text: ","
              - link "purring" [ref=e435] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Purr
              - text: ", trilling,"
              - link "hissing" [ref=e436] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/hiss
              - text: ","
              - link "growling" [ref=e437] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Growling
              - text: ","
              - link "grunting" [ref=e438] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/grunt
              - text: ","
              - link "body language" [ref=e439] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cat_body_language
              - text: ", and"
              - link "scent marking" [ref=e440] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scent_rubbing
              - text: . It can hear sounds too faint or too high in
              - link "frequency" [ref=e441] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frequency
              - text: for human ears, such as those made by
              - link "small mammals" [ref=e442] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Small_mammal
              - text: . It secretes and perceives
              - link "pheromones" [ref=e443] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pheromone
              - text: .
              - link "Cat intelligence" [ref=e444] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cat_intelligence
              - text: is evident in its ability to adapt, learn through observation, and solve problems. The domestic cat is the only
              - link "domesticated" [ref=e445] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Domestication
              - link "species" [ref=e446] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Species
              - text: of the family Felidae.
            - paragraph [ref=e447]:
              - text: Advances in
              - link "archaeology" [ref=e448] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archaeology
              - text: and
              - link "genetics" [ref=e449] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Genetics
              - text: have shown that the
              - link "domestication of the cat" [ref=e450] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Domestication_of_the_cat
              - text: started in the
              - link "Near East" [ref=e451] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Near_East
              - text: around 7500 BCE. Today, the domestic cat occurs across the globe and is valued by humans for companionship and its ability to kill
              - link "vermin" [ref=e452] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vermin
              - text: . It is commonly kept as a
              - link "pet" [ref=e453] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pet
              - text: ","
              - link "working cat" [ref=e454] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Working_cat
              - text: ", and"
              - link "pedigreed cat" [ref=e455] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pedigreed_cat
              - text: shown at
              - link "cat fancy" [ref=e456] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cat_fancy
              - text: events. Out of the estimated 600 million domestic cats worldwide, 400 million reside in Asia, including 58 million in China. About 73.8 million cats are estimated to live in the United States, and about 10.9 million cats in the United Kingdom. It also ranges freely as a
              - link "feral cat" [ref=e457] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Feral_cat
              - text: ", avoiding human contact. Pet abandonment contributes to increasing of the global feral cat population, which has driven the decline of"
              - link "bird" [ref=e458] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bird
              - text: ","
              - link "mammal" [ref=e459] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mammal
              - text: ", and"
              - link "reptile" [ref=e460] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reptile
              - text: species.
              - link "Population control" [ref=e461] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Animal_population_control
              - text: includes
              - link "spaying" [ref=e462] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spaying
              - text: and
              - link "neutering" [ref=e463] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neutering
              - text: .
          - region [ref=e464]:
            - heading "Etymology and naming" [level=2] [ref=e466]
            - paragraph [ref=e467]:
              - text: The origin of the English word cat,
              - link "Old English" [ref=e468] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_English
              - generic "Old English (ca. 450-1100)-language text" [ref=e469]: catt
              - text: ", is thought to be the"
              - link "Late Latin" [ref=e470] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Late_Latin
              - text: word
              - generic "Latin-language text" [ref=e471]: cattus

                  - link "mural" [ref=e966] [cursor=pointer]:

                  - text: in an Egyptian tomb dating to the 15th century BCE.
              - paragraph [ref=e967]:
                - text: It was long thought that the
                - link "domestication of the cat" [ref=e968] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Domestication_of_the_cat
                - text: began in
                - link "ancient Egypt" [ref=e969] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ancient_Egypt
                - text: ", where cats were venerated from around 3100 BCE."
                - superscript [ref=e970]:
                  - link "[39]" [ref=e971] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#cite_note-40"
                - superscript [ref=e973]:
                  - link "[40]" [ref=e974] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#cite_note-Malek1997-41"
                - text: However, the earliest known indication for the
                - link "taming" [ref=e976] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taming
                - text: of an African wildcat was
                - link "excavated" [ref=e977] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Excavation_(archaeology)
                - text: close by a human
                - link "Neolithic" [ref=e978] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neolithic
                - text: grave in
                - link "Shillourokambos" [ref=e979] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shillourokambos
                - text: ", southern"
                - link "Cyprus" [ref=e980] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cyprus
                - text: ", dating to about 7500–7200 BCE. Since there is no evidence of native mammalian"
                - link "fauna" [ref=e981] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fauna
                - text: on Cyprus, the inhabitants of this village most likely brought the cat and other wild mammals to the island from the West Asian mainland.
                - superscript [ref=e982]:
                  - link "[41]" [ref=e983] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#cite_note-Vigne_al2004-42"
                - text: Scientists therefore assume that African wildcats were attracted to early human settlements in the
                - link "Fertile Crescent" [ref=e985] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fertile_Crescent
                - text: by rodents, in particular the
                - link "house mouse" [ref=e986] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House_mouse
                - text: (Mus musculus), and were tamed by Neolithic farmers. This
                - link "mutual" [ref=e987] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mutualism_(biology)
                - text: relationship between early farmers and tamed cats lasted thousands of years. As
                - link "agricultural practices" [ref=e988] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agricultural_practices
                - text: spread, so did tame and domesticated cats.
                - superscript [ref=e989]:
                  - link "[38]" [ref=e990] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#cite_note-DriscollMenotti-Raymond2007-39"
                - superscript [ref=e992]:

                    - /url: "#cite_note-Driscoll_al2009-43"
                - text: Wildcats of Egypt contributed to the maternal
                - link "gene pool" [ref=e995] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gene_pool
                - text: of the domestic cat at a later time.
                - superscript [ref=e996]:

              - paragraph [ref=e999]:
                - text: The earliest known evidence for the occurrence of the domestic cat in Greece dates to around 1200 BCE. Greek,
                - link "Phoenician" [ref=e1000] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phoenicia
                - text: ","
                - link "Carthaginian" [ref=e1001] [cursor=pointer]:

                - text: and
                - link "Etruscan" [ref=e1002] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Etrusca
                - text: traders introduced it to southern Europe.
                - superscript [ref=e1003]:
                  - link "[44]" [ref=e1004] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#cite_note-Faure2009-45"
                - text: By the 5th century BCE, it was a familiar animal around settlements in
                - link "Magna Graecia" [ref=e1006] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magna_Graecia
                - text: and
                - link "Etruria" [ref=e1007] [cursor=pointer]:

                - text: .
                - superscript [ref=e1008]:

                - link "Roman Empire" [ref=e1011] [cursor=pointer]:

                - text: and
                - link "Sardinia" [ref=e1013] [cursor=pointer]:

                - text: .
                - superscript [ref=e1014]:
                  - link "[46]" [ref=e1015] [cursor=pointer]:

                - link "Western Roman Empire" [ref=e1017] [cursor=pointer]:

                - link "Baltic Sea" [ref=e1018] [cursor=pointer]:

                - text: port in northern Germany.

                  - link "[43]" [ref=e1020] [cursor=pointer]:

              - paragraph [ref=e1022]:
                - text: The
                - link "leopard cat" [ref=e1023] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leopard_cat
                - text: (Prionailurus bengalensis) was
                - link "tamed" [ref=e1024] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tamed
                - text: independently in China around 5500 BCE. This line of a partially domesticated cat left no trace in the domestic cat populations of today.
                - superscript [ref=e1025]:

                    - /url: "#cite_note-48"
              - paragraph [ref=e1028]:
                - text: During domestication, cats have undergone only minor changes in anatomy and behavior, and they are still capable of surviving in the wild. Several natural behaviors and characteristics of wildcats may have
                - link "pre-adapted" [ref=e1029] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Preadaptation
                - text: them for domestication as pets. These traits include their small size, social nature, obvious body language, love of play, and high intelligence. Their rigorous grooming habits and instinct to bury their bodily waste make them generally much less messy than other domesticated animals. Captive
                - link "Leopardus" [ref=e1031] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leopardus
                - text: cats may also display affectionate behavior toward humans but are not domesticated.
                - superscript [ref=e1032]:
                  - link "[48]" [ref=e1033] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#cite_note-CameronBeaumont-49"
                - text: House cats may mate with feral cats.

                - text: of these breeds varies between regions, and is lowest in purebred populations, which show more than 20 deleterious
                - link "genetic disorders" [ref=e1049] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Genetic_disorder
                - text: .

                - text: The domestic cat has a smaller
                - link "skull" [ref=e1075] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skull
                - text: and shorter bones than the
                - link "European wildcat" [ref=e1076] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_wildcat
                - text: .
                - superscript [ref=e1077]:
                  - link "[55]" [ref=e1078] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#cite_note-OConnor-56"
                - text: It averages about 46 cm (18 in) in head-to-body length and 23–25 cm (9.1–9.8 in) in height, with about 30 cm (12 in) long tails. Males are larger than females.
                - superscript [ref=e1080]:
                  - link "[56]" [ref=e1081] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#cite_note-WCoW-57"

            - region [ref=e1086]:
              - heading "Skeleton" [level=3] [ref=e1088]
              - paragraph [ref=e1089]:
                - text: Cats have seven
                - link "cervical vertebrae" [ref=e1090] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cervical_vertebrae
                - text: (as do most
                - link "mammals" [ref=e1091] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mammal
                - text: ); 13
                - link "thoracic vertebrae" [ref=e1092] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thoracic_vertebrae
                - text: (humans have 12); seven
                - link "lumbar vertebrae" [ref=e1093] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lumbar_vertebrae
                - text: (humans have five); three
                - link "sacral vertebrae" [ref=e1094] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sacrum
                - text: (as do most mammals, but humans have five); and a variable number of
                - link "caudal vertebrae" [ref=e1095] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caudal_vertebrae
                - text: in the tail (humans have only three to five vestigial caudal vertebrae, fused into an internal
                - link "coccyx" [ref=e1096] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coccyx
                - text: ).
                - superscript [ref=e1097]:
                  - link "[57]" [ref=e1098] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#cite_note-Walker-58"
                - superscript [ref=e1100]:
                  - 'generic "Page / location: 11" [ref=e1101]': ": 11"
                - text: The extra lumbar and thoracic vertebrae account for the cat's spinal mobility and flexibility. Attached to the spine are 13 ribs, the shoulder, and the
                - link "pelvis" [ref=e1102] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pelvis
                - text: .
                - superscript [ref=e1103]:
                  - link "[57]" [ref=e1104] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#cite_note-Walker-58"
                - superscript [ref=e1106]:
                  - 'generic "Page / location: 16" [ref=e1107]': ": 16"
                - text: Unlike human arms, cat forelimbs are attached to the shoulder by free-floating
                - link "clavicle" [ref=e1108] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clavicle
                - text: bones which allow them to pass their body through any space into which they can fit their head.
                - superscript [ref=e1109]:
                  - link "[58]" [ref=e1110] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#cite_note-Gillis_2002-59"
            - region [ref=e1112]:
              - heading "Skull" [level=3] [ref=e1114]
              - figure "Cat skull" [ref=e1115]:
                - link [ref=e1116] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Cat_skull.jpg
              - paragraph [ref=e1119]:
                - text: The cat skull is unusual among mammals in having very large
                - link "eye sockets" [ref=e1120] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eye_socket
                - text: and a powerful specialized jaw.
                - superscript [ref=e1121]:
                  - link "[59]" [ref=e1122] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#cite_note-Case-60"
                - superscript [ref=e1124]:
                  - 'generic "Page / location: 35" [ref=e1125]': ": 35"
                - text: Two long
                - link "canine teeth" [ref=e1126] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canine_tooth
                - text: for killing and tearing prey can stab between two of the prey's
                - link "vertebrae" [ref=e1127] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vertebra
                - text: and sever its
                - link "spinal cord" [ref=e1128] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spinal_cord
                - text: ", causing"
                - link "paralysis" [ref=e1129] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paralysis
                - text: and death.
                - superscript [ref=e1130]:
                  - link "[60]" [ref=e1131] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#cite_note-Smith1992-61"
                - text: Compared to other felines, domestic cats have narrowly spaced canine teeth relative to the size of their jaw, which is an adaptation to their preferred prey of small rodents, which have small vertebrae.
                - superscript [ref=e1133]:
                  - link "[60]" [ref=e1134] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#cite_note-Smith1992-61"
              - paragraph [ref=e1136]:
                - text: The
                - link "premolar" [ref=e1137] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Premolar
                - text: and first
                - link "molar" [ref=e1138] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Molar_(tooth)
                - text: together compose the
                - link "carnassial" [ref=e1139] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carnassial
                - text: pair on each side of the mouth, which efficiently shears meat into small pieces, like a pair of scissors. These are vital in feeding, because cats' small molars cannot chew food effectively, and cats are largely incapable of mastication.
                - superscript [ref=e1140]:
                  - link "[59]" [ref=e1141] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#cite_note-Case-60"
                - superscript [ref=e1143]:
                  - 'generic "Page / location: 37" [ref=e1144]': ": 37"
                - text: Cats tend to have better dental health than most humans, with decay generally less likely because of a thicker protective layer of
                - link "enamel" [ref=e1145] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tooth_enamel
                - text: ", a less damaging saliva, less retention of food particles between teeth, and a diet mostly devoid of sugar. Nonetheless, they are subject to occasional tooth loss and infection."
                - superscript [ref=e1146]:
                  - link "[61]" [ref=e1147] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#cite_note-Carr1978-62"
            - region [ref=e1149]:
              - heading "Claws" [level=3] [ref=e1151]
              - figure "Cat's claw" [ref=e1152]:
                - link [ref=e1153] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Cat_claw_closeup.jpg
              - paragraph [ref=e1156]:
                - text: Cats have protractible and retractable claws.
                - superscript [ref=e1157]:
                  - link "[62]" [ref=e1158] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#cite_note-Kitchener2010-63"
                - text: In their normal, relaxed position, the claws are sheathed with the skin and fur around the paw's toe pads. This keeps the claws sharp by preventing wear from contact with the ground and allows for the silent stalking of prey. The claws on the forefeet are typically sharper than those on the hindfeet.
                - superscript [ref=e1160]:
                  - link "[63]" [ref=e1161] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#cite_note-Armes_1900-64"
                - text: Cats can voluntarily extend their claws, such as in hunting, fighting, climbing,
                - link "kneading" [ref=e1163] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kneading_(cats)
                - text: ", or for extra traction on soft surfaces. Cats shed the outside layer of their claw sheaths when scratching rough surfaces."
                - superscript [ref=e1164]:
                  - link "[64]" [ref=e1165] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#cite_note-pmid19422432-65"
              - paragraph [ref=e1167]:
                - text: Most cats have five claws on their front paws and four on their rear paws. The
                - link "dewclaw" [ref=e1168] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dewclaw
                - text: is
                - link "proximal" [ref=e1169] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proximal
                - text: to the other claws. More proximally is a protrusion which appears to be a sixth "finger". This special feature of the front paws on the inside of the wrists has no function in normal walking but is thought to be an antiskidding device used while jumping. Some cat breeds are prone to having extra digits ("
                - link "polydactyly" [ref=e1170] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polydactyl_cat
                - text: "\")."
                - superscript [ref=e1171]:
                  - link "[65]" [ref=e1172] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#cite_note-Danforth1947-66"
            - region [ref=e1174]:
              - heading "Ambulation" [level=3] [ref=e1176]
              - paragraph [ref=e1177]:
                - text: The cat is
                - link "digitigrade" [ref=e1178] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Digitigrade
                - text: . It walks on the toes, with the bones of the feet making up the lower part of the visible leg.
                - superscript [ref=e1179]:
                  - link "[66]" [ref=e1180] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#cite_note-Pocock1917-67"
                - text: Unlike most mammals, it uses a "pacing"
                - link "gait" [ref=e1182] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gait
                - text: "that alternates both legs together on each side. It registers directly by placing each hind paw close to the track of the corresponding fore paw, minimizing noise and visible tracks. This also provides sure footing for hind paws when navigating rough terrain. As it speeds up from walking to trotting, its gait changes to a \"diagonal\" gait: The diagonally opposite hind and fore legs move simultaneously."
                - superscript [ref=e1183]:
                  - link "[67]" [ref=e1184] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#cite_note-Christensen_2004-68"
            - region [ref=e1186]:
              - heading "Balance" [level=3] [ref=e1188]
              - figure "A cat is perched on a tree branch, having climbed up for exploration, escape, or hunting." [ref=e1189]:
                - link [ref=e1190] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Cat_in_tree03.jpg
              - paragraph [ref=e1193]:
                - text: Cats are generally fond of perching in high places. This may be a concealed hunting site such as a tree branch, for domestic cats to pounce upon prey. They favor a superior observation point over territory. A cat falling from up to 3 m (9.8 ft) can right itself and land on its paws.
                - superscript [ref=e1194]:
                  - link "[68]" [ref=e1195] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#cite_note-Kent_et_al._2010-69"
              - paragraph [ref=e1197]:
                - text: During a lofty fall, a cat reflexively twists and rights itself to land on its feet using its acute sense of balance and flexibility. This reflex is known as the
                - link "cat righting reflex" [ref=e1198] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cat_righting_reflex
                - text: .
                - superscript [ref=e1199]:
                  - link "[69]" [ref=e1200] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#cite_note-70"
                - text: A cat always rights itself in the same way, and it has enough time in falls of at least 90 cm (3.0 ft).
                - superscript [ref=e1202]:
                  - link "[70]" [ref=e1203] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#cite_note-Nguyen_1998-71"
                - text: This has been investigated as the "
                - link "falling cat problem" [ref=e1205] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Falling_cat_problem
                - text: "\"."
                - superscript [ref=e1206]:
                  - link "[71]" [ref=e1207] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#cite_note-72"
            - region [ref=e1209]:

                - link "ASIP" [ref=e1224] [cursor=pointer]:

                - link "microsatellite" [ref=e1228] [cursor=pointer]:

                - link "clone" [ref=e1229] [cursor=pointer]:

                - link "linkage analysis" [ref=e1230] [cursor=pointer]:

                - text: on 89 domestic cats segregated for
                - link "melanism" [ref=e1231] [cursor=pointer]:

                - link "cosegregation" [ref=e1232] [cursor=pointer]:

            - region [ref=e1236]:
              - heading "Diet" [level=3] [ref=e1238]
              - paragraph [ref=e1239]:
                - text: The cat is an obligate carnivore and has adapted to a low-fibre highly digestible meat diet. Cats have fewer
                - link "enzymes" [ref=e1240] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enzyme
                - text: capable of metabolising
                - link "carbohydrates" [ref=e1241] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carbohydrates
                - text: compared to omnivores. The cat lacks the ability to convert
                - link "carotenoids" [ref=e1242] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carotenoids
                - text: to vitamin A; has an inability to synthesise enough vitamin D; inability to synthesise
                - link "niacin" [ref=e1243] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Niacin
                - text: from
                - link "tryptophan" [ref=e1244] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tryptophan
                - text: ; inability to synthesise
                - link "cysteine" [ref=e1245] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cysteine
                - text: ","
                - link "citrulline" [ref=e1246] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Citrulline
                - text: ", and"
                - link "methionine" [ref=e1247] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Methionine
                - text: ; lacks
                - link "glucokinase" [ref=e1248] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glucokinase
                - text: activity; and an intolerance to
                - link "glutamic acid" [ref=e1249] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glutamic_acid
                - text: (which is low in animal tissue and high in plant matter).
                - link "Taurine" [ref=e1250] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taurine
                - text: and
                - link "arginine" [ref=e1251] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arginine
                - text: are essential for cats. Due to the inability to synthesise adequate amounts of citrulline a single meal lacking in arginine can be fatal to a cat. Cats cannot produce enough taurine and require dietary taurine; a lack of taurine will cause a cat to develop
                - link "dilated cardiomyopathy" [ref=e1252] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dilated_cardiomyopathy
                - text: . Commercial cat diets historically were lacking in taurine and dilated cardiomyopathy was a common issue until it was linked to taurine deficiency in a 1987 study.
                - superscript [ref=e1253]:
                  - link "[73]" [ref=e1254] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#cite_note-Fascetti_2023-74"
          - region [ref=e1256]:
            - heading "Senses" [level=2] [ref=e1258]
            - note [ref=e1259]:
              - text: "Main article:"
              - link "Cat senses" [ref=e1260] [cursor=pointer]:

            - region [ref=e1261]:
              - heading "Vision" [level=3] [ref=e1263]
              - figure [ref=e1264]:
                - link [ref=e1265] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Tabby_cat_with_visible_nictitating_membrane.jpg
                  - img "A tabby cat with a third, translucent eyelid covering part of either eye" [ref=e1266]
                - generic [ref=e1267]:
                  - text: A cat's
                  - link "nictitating membrane" [ref=e1268] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nictitating_membrane
                  - text: is exposed as it blinks.
              - paragraph [ref=e1269]:
                - text: Cats have excellent night vision and can see at one sixth the light level required for human vision.
                - superscript [ref=e1270]:
                  - link "[59]" [ref=e1271] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#cite_note-Case-60"
                - superscript [ref=e1273]:
                  - 'generic "Page / location: 43" [ref=e1274]': ": 43"
                - text: This is partly the result of cat eyes having a
                - link "tapetum lucidum" [ref=e1276] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tapetum_lucidum
                - text: ", which reflects any light that passes through the"
                - link "retina" [ref=e1277] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Retina
                - text: back into the eye, thereby increasing the eye's sensitivity to dim light.
                - superscript [ref=e1278]:
                  - link "[74]" [ref=e1279] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#cite_note-75"
                - text: Large pupils are an adaptation to dim light. The domestic cat has
                - link "slit pupils" [ref=e1281] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pupil#In_other_animals
                - text: ", which allow it to focus bright light without"
                - link "chromatic aberration" [ref=e1282] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromatic_aberration
                - text: .
                - superscript [ref=e1283]:
                  - link "[75]" [ref=e1284] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#cite_note-76"
                - text: At low light, a cat's pupils expand to cover most of the exposed surface of its eyes.
                - superscript [ref=e1286]:
                  - link "[76]" [ref=e1287] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#cite_note-77"
                - text: The domestic cat has rather poor
                - link "color vision" [ref=e1289] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Color_vision
                - text: and only two types of
                - link "cone cells" [ref=e1290] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cone_cell
                - text: ", optimized for sensitivity to blue and yellowish green; its ability to distinguish between red and green is limited."
                - superscript [ref=e1291]:
                  - link "[77]" [ref=e1292] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#cite_note-78"
                - text: A response to middle wavelengths from a system other than the
                - link "rod cells" [ref=e1294] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rod_cell
                - text: might be due to a third type of cone. This appears to be an adaptation to low light levels rather than representing true
                - link "trichromatic" [ref=e1295] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichromacy
                - text: vision.
                - superscript [ref=e1296]:
                  - link "[78]" [ref=e1297] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#cite_note-79"
                - text: Cats have a
                - link "nictitating membrane" [ref=e1299] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nictitating_membrane
                - text: ", allowing them to blink without hindering their vision."
            - region [ref=e1300]:
              - heading "Hearing" [level=3] [ref=e1302]
              - paragraph [ref=e1303]:
                - text: The domestic cat's hearing is most acute in the range of 500
                - link "Hz" [ref=e1304] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hz
                - text: to 32 kHz.
                - superscript [ref=e1305]:
                  - link "[79]" [ref=e1306] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#cite_note-80"
                - text: It can detect an extremely broad range of frequencies ranging from 55 Hz to 79 kHz, whereas humans can only detect frequencies between 20 Hz and 20 kHz. It can hear a range of 10.5
                - link "octaves" [ref=e1308] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Octave
                - text: ", compared to about 9 octaves for humans and dogs."
                - superscript [ref=e1309]:
                  - link "[80]" [ref=e1310] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#cite_note-81"
                - superscript [ref=e1312]:
                  - link "[81]" [ref=e1313] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#cite_note-82"
                - text: Its hearing sensitivity is enhanced by its large movable outer ears, the
                - link "pinnae" [ref=e1315] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pinna_(anatomy)
                - text: ", which amplify sounds and help detect the location of a noise. It can detect"
                - link "ultrasound" [ref=e1316] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ultrasound
                - text: ", including ultrasonic calls from"
                - link "rodent" [ref=e1317] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rodent
                - text: prey.
                - superscript [ref=e1318]:
                  - link "[82]" [ref=e1319] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#cite_note-Sunquist-83"
                - superscript [ref=e1321]:
                  - link "[83]" [ref=e1322] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#cite_note-84"
                - text: Research has shown that cats have socio-spatial cognitive abilities to create mental maps of familiar people's locations based on hearing their voices.
                - superscript [ref=e1324]:
                  - link "[84]" [ref=e1325] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#cite_note-85"
            - region [ref=e1327]:
              - heading "Smell" [level=3] [ref=e1329]
              - paragraph [ref=e1330]:
                - text: Cats have an acute sense of smell, due in part to their well-developed
                - link "olfactory bulb" [ref=e1331] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Olfactory_bulb
                - text: and a large surface of
                - link "olfactory mucosa" [ref=e1332] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Olfactory_mucosa
                - text: ", about 5.8 cm"
                - superscript [ref=e1333]: "2"
                - text: (0.90 in
                - superscript [ref=e1334]: "2"
                - text: ) in area, which is about twice that of humans.
                - superscript [ref=e1335]:
                  - link "[85]" [ref=e1336] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#cite_note-Moulton_1967-86"
                - text: Cats and many other animals have a
                - link "Jacobson's organ" [ref=e1338] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacobson's_organ
                - text: in their mouths that is used in the behavioral process of
                - link "flehmening" [ref=e1339] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flehmen_response
                - text: . It allows them to sense certain aromas in a way that humans cannot. Cats are sensitive to
                - link "pheromones" [ref=e1340] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cat_pheromone
                - text: such as
                - link "3-mercapto-3-methylbutan-1-ol" [ref=e1341] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/3-mercapto-3-methylbutan-1-ol
                - text: ","
                - superscript [ref=e1342]:
                  - link "[86]" [ref=e1343] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#cite_note-felinine-87"
                - text: which they use to communicate through
                - link "urine spraying" [ref=e1345] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Urine_spraying
                - text: and marking with
                - link "scent glands" [ref=e1346] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scent_gland
                - text: .
                - superscript [ref=e1347]:
                  - link "[87]" [ref=e1348] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#cite_note-Sommerville-88"
                - text: Many cats also respond strongly to plants that contain
                - link "nepetalactone" [ref=e1350] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nepetalactone
                - text: ", especially"
                - link "catnip" [ref=e1351] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catnip
                - text: ", which they can detect at less than one part per billion."
                - superscript [ref=e1352]:
                  - link "[88]" [ref=e1353] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#cite_note-89"
                - text: About 70–80% of cats are affected by nepetalactone.
                - superscript [ref=e1355]:
                  - link "[89]" [ref=e1356] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#cite_note-90"
                - text: This response is also produced by other plants, such as silver vine (
                - link "Actinidia polygama" [ref=e1359] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Actinidia_polygama
                - text: ) and the herb
                - link "valerian" [ref=e1360] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Valerian_(herb)
                - text: ; it may be caused by the smell of these plants mimicking a pheromone and stimulating cats' social or sexual behaviors.
                - superscript [ref=e1361]:

            - region [ref=e1364]:
              - heading "Taste" [level=3] [ref=e1366]
              - paragraph [ref=e1367]:
                - text: Cats have about 470
                - link "taste buds" [ref=e1368] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taste_bud
                - text: ", compared to more than 9,000 on the human tongue."
                - superscript [ref=e1369]:
                  - link "[91]" [ref=e1370] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#cite_note-sch-92"
                - text: Domestic and wild cats share a
                - link "taste receptor gene mutation" [ref=e1372] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taste_receptor#Loss_of_function
                - text: that keeps their sweet taste buds from binding to sugary molecules, leaving them with no ability to taste
                - link "sweetness" [ref=e1373] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sweetness
                - text: .
                - superscript [ref=e1374]:
                  - link "[92]" [ref=e1375] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#cite_note-93"
                - text: But they do have taste bud receptors specialized for
                - link "acids" [ref=e1377] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Acid
                - text: ","
                - link "amino acids" [ref=e1378] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amino_acid
                - text: such as the constituents of protein, and bitter tastes.
                - superscript [ref=e1379]:
                  - link "[93]" [ref=e1380] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#cite_note-Bradshaw2006-94"
              - paragraph [ref=e1382]:
                - text: Cats' taste buds possess the receptors needed to detect
                - link "umami" [ref=e1383] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Umami
                - text: . However, these receptors contain molecular changes that make them taste umami differently from humans. In humans, they detect the amino acids
                - link "glutamic acid" [ref=e1384] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glutamic_acid
                - text: and
                - link "aspartic acid" [ref=e1385] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aspartic_acid
                - text: ; but in cats, they instead detect
                - link "inosine monophosphate" [ref=e1386] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inosine_monophosphate
                - text: and
                - link "histidine" [ref=e1387] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Histidine
                - text: .
                - superscript [ref=e1388]:
                  - link "[94]" [ref=e1389] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#cite_note-McGrane_Gibbs_Hernangomez_de_Alvaro_Dunlop-95"
                - text: These molecules are particularly enriched in
                - link "tuna" [ref=e1391] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tuna
                - text: .
                - superscript [ref=e1392]:
                  - link "[94]" [ref=e1393] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#cite_note-McGrane_Gibbs_Hernangomez_de_Alvaro_Dunlop-95"
                - text: Researchers argue why cats find tuna so
                - link "palatable" [ref=e1395] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palatability
                - text: ": \"the specific combination of the high IMP and free histidine contents of tuna, which produces a strong umami taste synergy that is highly preferred by cats.\""
                - superscript [ref=e1396]:
                  - link "[94]" [ref=e1397] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#cite_note-McGrane_Gibbs_Hernangomez_de_Alvaro_Dunlop-95"
                - text: One researcher said, "I think umami is as important for cats as sweet is for humans."
                - superscript [ref=e1399]:
                  - link "[95]" [ref=e1400] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#cite_note-Science_Tuna_Cat-96"
              - paragraph [ref=e1402]:
                - text: Cats distinctly prefer food temperature around 38 °C (100 °F), similar to a fresh kill. Some cats reject cold food, which would signal to the cat that the prey is long dead and therefore possibly toxic or decomposing.
                - superscript [ref=e1403]:
                  - link "[91]" [ref=e1404] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#cite_note-sch-92"
            - region [ref=e1406]:
              - heading "Whiskers" [level=3] [ref=e1408]
              - figure "The whiskers of a cat are highly sensitive to touch." [ref=e1409]:
                - link [ref=e1410] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Kittyply_edit1.jpg
              - paragraph [ref=e1413]:
                - text: To aid with navigation and sensation, cats have dozens of movable
                - link "whiskers (vibrissae)" [ref=e1414] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vibrissa
                - text: over their body, most prominently on their faces, as seen by the long, white lines diverging outwards from its nose. These provide information on the width of gaps and on the location of objects in the dark, both by touching objects directly and by sensing air currents. They trigger protective
                - link "blink reflexes" [ref=e1415] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blink_reflex
                - text: to protect the eyes from damage.
                - superscript [ref=e1416]:

          - region [ref=e1421]:
            - heading "Behavior" [level=2] [ref=e1423]
            - note [ref=e1424]:
              - text: "See also:"
              - link "Cat behavior" [ref=e1425] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cat_behavior
            - paragraph [ref=e1426]:
              - text: Outdoor cats are active both day and
              - link "night" [ref=e1427] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nocturnal_animal
              - text: ", although they tend to be slightly more active at night."
              - superscript [ref=e1428]:
                - link "[96]" [ref=e1429] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: "#cite_note-97"
              - text: Domestic cats spend the majority of their time in the vicinity of their homes, but they can range a radius of many hundreds of meters. They establish
              - link "territories" [ref=e1431] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Territory_(animal)
              - text: that vary considerably in size, in one study ranging 7–28 ha (17–69 acres).
              - superscript [ref=e1432]:
                - link "[97]" [ref=e1433] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: "#cite_note-98"
              - text: The timing of cats' activity is quite flexible and varied; but being low-light predators, they are generally
              - link "crepuscular" [ref=e1435] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crepuscular_animal
              - text: ", which means they tend to be more active near dawn and dusk. However, house cats' behavior is also influenced by human activity, and they may adapt to their owners' sleeping patterns to some extent."
              - superscript [ref=e1436]:
                - link "[98]" [ref=e1437] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: "#cite_note-99"
              - superscript [ref=e1439]:
                - link "[99]" [ref=e1440] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: "#cite_note-100"
            - paragraph [ref=e1442]:
              - text: Cats conserve energy by sleeping more than most animals, especially as they grow older. The daily duration of sleep varies, usually between 12 and 16 hours, with 13 to 14 being the average. Some cats can sleep as much as 20 hours. The term "cat nap" for a short rest refers to the cat's tendency to fall asleep (lightly) for a brief period. Short periods of
              - link "rapid eye movement sleep" [ref=e1443] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rapid_eye_movement_sleep
              - text: are often accompanied by muscle twitches, which suggests they are dreaming.
              - superscript [ref=e1444]:
                - link "[100]" [ref=e1445] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: "#cite_note-101"
            - paragraph [ref=e1447]:
              - text: Behavioral and personality traits depend on a complex interplay between genetic and environmental factors. Scientific evidence does not support the popular belief that those traits are linked to coat colors.
              - superscript [ref=e1448]:
                - link "[101]" [ref=e1449] [cursor=pointer]:

            - region [ref=e1457]:
              - heading "Sociability" [level=3] [ref=e1459]
              - paragraph [ref=e1460]:
                - text: The social behavior of the domestic cat ranges from widely dispersed individuals to
                - link "feral cat colonies" [ref=e1461] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Feral_cat_colony
                - text: that gather around a food source, based on groups of co-operating females.
                - superscript [ref=e1462]:
                  - link "[104]" [ref=e1463] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#cite_note-Crowell-davis2004-105"
                - superscript [ref=e1465]:
                  - link "[105]" [ref=e1466] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#cite_note-Liberg_al2014-106"
                - text: Within such groups, one cat is usually dominant over the others.
                - superscript [ref=e1468]:
                  - link "[106]" [ref=e1469] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#cite_note-107"
                - text: Each cat in a colony holds a distinct territory, with sexually active males having the largest territories, which are about 10 times larger than those of female cats and may overlap with several females' territories. These territories are marked by
                - link "urine spraying" [ref=e1471] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Urine_spraying
                - text: ", rubbing objects at head height with secretions from facial glands, and by"
                - link "defecation" [ref=e1472] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Defecation
                - text: .
                - superscript [ref=e1473]:
                  - link "[87]" [ref=e1474] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#cite_note-Sommerville-88"
                - text: Between these territories are neutral areas where cats watch and greet one another without territorial conflicts. Outside these neutral areas, territory holders usually chase away stranger cats, at first by staring, hissing, and
                - link "growling" [ref=e1476] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Growling
                - text: ", and, if that does not work, by short and violent, noisy attacks. Because cats do not have a social survival strategy or"
                - link "herd behavior" [ref=e1477] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herd_behavior
                - text: ", they always hunt alone."
                - superscript [ref=e1478]:
                  - link "[107]" [ref=e1479] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#cite_note-Bradshaw-108"
              - figure "Two kittens lying side by side, an instinctive behavior that offers both comfort and protection" [ref=e1481]:
                - link [ref=e1482] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Kittens_resting_close_together_for_warmth_and_security.jpg
                  - img "Two kittens resting side by side, an instinctive behavior that offers both protection and comfort" [ref=e1483]
              - paragraph [ref=e1485]:
                - text: Life in proximity to humans and other domestic animals has led to a symbiotic social adaptation in cats, and cats may express great affection toward humans or other animals.
                - link "Ethologically" [ref=e1486] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethology
                - text: ", a cat's human keeper functions as a mother surrogate."
                - superscript [ref=e1487]:
                  - link "[108]" [ref=e1488] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#cite_note-109"
                - text: Adult cats live in a type of extended kittenhood, a form of behavioral
                - link "neoteny" [ref=e1490] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neoteny
                - text: . Their high-pitched sounds may mimic the cries of a hungry human infant, making them particularly difficult for humans to ignore.
                - superscript [ref=e1491]:
                  - link "[109]" [ref=e1492] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#cite_note-McComb_2009-110"
                - text: Some pet cats are poorly socialized. In particular, older cats may show aggressiveness toward newly arrived kittens, which includes biting and scratching; this type of behavior is known as feline asocial aggression.
                - superscript [ref=e1494]:
                  - link "[110]" [ref=e1495] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#cite_note-Levine_2005-111"
              - paragraph [ref=e1497]:
                - link "Redirected aggression" [ref=e1498] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Redirected_aggression
                - text: is a common form of aggression that can occur in multiple cat households. In redirected aggression, a cat is usually agitated by a stimulus such as a sight, sound, or other trigger that causes heightened anxiety or arousal; if the cat cannot attack the original stimulus, it may redirect its aggression toward the nearest cat, pet, human, or other being.
                - superscript [ref=e1499]:
                  - link "[111]" [ref=e1500] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#cite_note-Horwitz-112"
                - superscript [ref=e1502]:
                  - link "[112]" [ref=e1503] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#cite_note-Behaviorist-113"

                - text: Domestic cats'
                - link "scent rubbing" [ref=e1506] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scent_rubbing
                - text: behavior toward humans or other cats is thought to be a feline means of social bonding.

                - link "trilling" [ref=e1544] [cursor=pointer]:

                - superscript [ref=e1545]:

                - text: Their
                - link "body language" [ref=e1548] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cat_body_language
                - text: ", including position of ears and tail, relaxation of the whole body, and kneading of the paws, are all indicators of mood. The tail and ears are particularly important social signal mechanisms; a raised tail indicates a friendly greeting, and flattened ears indicate hostility. Tail-raising also indicates the cat's position in the group's"
                - link "social hierarchy" [ref=e1549] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Social_hierarchy
                - text: ", with dominant individuals raising their tails less often than subordinate ones."

                - text: Feral cats are generally silent.

                - superscript [ref=e1556]:
                  - 'generic "Page / location: 208" [ref=e1557]': ": 208"
                - text: Nose-to-nose touching is also a common greeting and may be followed by
                - link "social grooming" [ref=e1558] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Social_grooming
                - text: ", which is solicited by one of the cats raising and tilting its head."
                - superscript [ref=e1559]:

              - paragraph [ref=e1562]:
                - link "Purring" [ref=e1563] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Purring
                - text: may have developed as an evolutionary advantage as a signaling mechanism of reassurance between mother cats and
                - link "nursing" [ref=e1564] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breastfeeding
                - text: kittens, who are thought to use it as a care-soliciting signal.
                - superscript [ref=e1565]:
                  - link "[117]" [ref=e1566] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#cite_note-bradshaw2012-118"
                - text: "Post-nursing cats also often purr as a sign of contentment: when being petted, becoming relaxed,"
                - superscript [ref=e1568]:
                  - link "[118]" [ref=e1569] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#cite_note-BruelKjaer-119"
                - superscript [ref=e1571]:
                  - link "[119]" [ref=e1572] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#cite_note-IsnareCom-120"
                - text: or eating. Although purring is popularly interpreted as indicative of pleasure, it has been recorded in a wide variety of circumstances, most of which involve physical contact between the cat and another, presumably trusted individual.
                - superscript [ref=e1574]:
                  - link "[117]" [ref=e1575] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#cite_note-bradshaw2012-118"
                - text: Some cats have been observed to purr continuously when chronically ill or in apparent pain.
                - superscript [ref=e1577]:
                  - link "[120]" [ref=e1578] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#cite_note-121"
              - paragraph [ref=e1580]:
                - text: The exact mechanism by which cats purr has long been elusive, but it has been proposed that purring is generated via a series of sudden build-ups and releases of pressure as the
                - link "glottis" [ref=e1581] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glottis
                - text: is opened and closed, which causes the
                - link "vocal folds" [ref=e1582] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vocal_folds
                - text: to separate forcefully. The
                - link "laryngeal muscles" [ref=e1583] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Larynx
                - text: in control of the glottis are thought to be driven by a
                - link "neural oscillator" [ref=e1584] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neural_oscillation
                - text: which generates a cycle of contraction and release every 30–40
                - link "milliseconds" [ref=e1585] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Millisecond
                - text: (giving a frequency of 33 to 25 Hz).
                - superscript [ref=e1586]:
                  - link "[117]" [ref=e1587] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#cite_note-bradshaw2012-118"
                - superscript [ref=e1589]:

                    - /url: "#cite_note-123"

                - text: based on 26 facial movements; each facial expression corresponds to different social functions that are probably influenced by domestication.

              - paragraph [ref=e1614]:
                - text: Cats are known for spending considerable amounts of time licking their coats to keep them clean.
                - superscript [ref=e1615]:

                - link "filiform papillae" [ref=e1621] [cursor=pointer]:

                - link "gut" [ref=e1628] [cursor=pointer]:

            - region [ref=e1632]:
              - heading "Cat intelligence" [level=3] [ref=e1634]
              - note [ref=e1635]:
                - text: "Main article:"
                - link "Cat intelligence" [ref=e1636] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cat_intelligence
              - figure "A cat uses problem-solving skills to open a door." [ref=e1637]:
                - generic [ref=e1639]:
                  - button "Play video" [ref=e1641] [cursor=pointer]
                  - generic [ref=e1643] [cursor=pointer]:

                    - text: 0:23
                - link:
                  - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Cat_opening_door.webm
              - paragraph [ref=e1646]:
                - text: Cat intelligence refers to a cat's ability to solve problems, adapt to its environment, learn new behaviors, and communicate its needs. Structurally, a cat's brain shares similarities with the human brain,
                - superscript [ref=e1647]:
                  - link "[129]" [ref=e1648] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#cite_note-Gross_20102-130"
                - text: containing around 250 million neurons in the cerebral cortex, which is responsible for complex processing.
                - superscript [ref=e1650]:
                  - link "[130]" [ref=e1651] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#cite_note-131"
                - text: Cats display
                - link "neuroplasticity" [ref=e1653] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neuroplasticity
                - text: allowing their brains to reorganize based on experiences. They have well-developed memory retaining information for a decade or longer. These memories are often intertwined with emotions, allowing cats to recall both positive and negative experiences associated with specific places.
                - superscript [ref=e1654]:
                  - link "[131]" [ref=e1655] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#cite_note-132"
                - text: While they excel in
                - link "observational learning" [ref=e1657] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Observational_learning
                - text: and problem-solving, studies conclude that they struggle with understanding cause-and-effect relationships in the same way that humans do.
                - superscript [ref=e1658]:
                  - link "[132]" [ref=e1659] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#cite_note-133"
              - paragraph [ref=e1661]:
                - text: Cat
                - link "intelligence" [ref=e1662] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Animal_cognition
                - text: study is mostly from consideration of the domesticated cat. Living in urban environments has exposed it to challenges that require adaptive behaviors, contributing to cognitive development.
                - superscript [ref=e1663]:
                  - link "[133]" [ref=e1664] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#cite_note-134"
                - text: Selective breeding and genetic changes have further influenced its intelligence.
                - superscript [ref=e1666]:
                  - link "[38]" [ref=e1667] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#cite_note-DriscollMenotti-Raymond2007-39"
                - text: Kittens learn essential survival skills by observing their mothers, while adult cats refine their abilities through
                - link "trial and error" [ref=e1669] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trial_and_error
                - text: .
                - superscript [ref=e1670]:
                  - link "[134]" [ref=e1671] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#cite_note-135"
            - region [ref=e1673]:
              - heading "Play" [level=3] [ref=e1675]
              - note [ref=e1676]:
                - text: "Main article:"
                - link "Cat play and toys" [ref=e1677] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cat_play_and_toys
              - figure "Kittens aged 14 weeks use fighting as a form of play." [ref=e1678]:

                - link:
                  - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Play_fight_between_cats.webmhd.webm
              - paragraph [ref=e1685]:
                - text: Domestic cats, especially young kittens, are known for their love of play. This behavior mimics hunting and is important in helping kittens learn to stalk, capture, and kill prey.
                - superscript [ref=e1686]:
                  - link "[135]" [ref=e1687] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#cite_note-136"
                - text: Cats also engage in
                - link "play fighting" [ref=e1689] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rough-and-tumble_play
                - text: ", both with each other and with humans. This behavior may be a way for cats to practice the skills needed for real combat, and it might also reduce the fear that they associate with launching attacks on other animals."
                - superscript [ref=e1690]:
                  - link "[136]" [ref=e1691] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#cite_note-137"
              - paragraph [ref=e1693]:
                - text: Cats also tend to play with toys more when they are hungry.
                - superscript [ref=e1694]:
                  - link "[137]" [ref=e1695] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#cite_note-138"
                - text: Owing to the close similarity between play and hunting, cats prefer to play with objects that resemble prey, such as small furry toys that move rapidly, but rapidly lose interest. They become
                - link "habituated" [ref=e1697] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Habituation
                - text: to a toy they have played with before.
                - superscript [ref=e1698]:
                  - link "[138]" [ref=e1699] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#cite_note-139"
                - text: String is often used as a toy, but if it is eaten, it can become caught at the base of the cat's tongue and then move into the
                - link "intestines" [ref=e1701] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Intestine
                - text: ", a medical emergency which can cause serious illness, even death."
                - superscript [ref=e1702]:
                  - link "[139]" [ref=e1703] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#cite_note-140"
            - region [ref=e1705]:
              - heading "Hunting and feeding" [level=3] [ref=e1707]
              - note [ref=e1708]:
